newsitem.title: CHINA: China not seen halting red-hot red chip offers.
newsitem.headline: China not seen halting red-hot red chip offers.

text.p: China has given no indication it wants to halt the listing of so-called red chips in Hong Kong, and the issues should not be seen as a loss of state assets, a BZW Asia Ltd executive said on Wednesday.
"There is no indication that China's regulators will put the brakes on red chips," BZW Asia managing director Huan Guocang told a news conference.
"I also don't believe there is a loss of state assets."
Huan said China was getting a relatively high price for the assets and still retained control after listing some of the shares in Hong Kong.

Red chips are Chinese-controlled companies that list shares on Hong Kong's stock exchange through corporate vehicles set up in the British colony. Red chips often have substantial assets that are based in China.
China's securities regulators have been concerned that some companies may be using Hong Kong corporate vehicles to offer stock and sidestep supervision by Beijing.
They have privately expressed concern that state assets may sold off at less than fair prices.
One such red chip offer was briefly delayed because Beijing regulators threatened to block it.
But many of the offers have ultimately been extremely successful.
Beijing Enterprises Holdings, a Beijing municipal government company with interests in toll roads, hotels, brewing and retailing, is offering some 150 million shares at HK$12.48 per share.

Potential investors in Hong Kong scooped up 400,000 application forms for the shares on the first day of subscription. Another 500,000 were printed, and the offer is expected to be more than 1,000 times oversubscribed.
Huan said this method of raising capital was preferable to selling assets to blue chip companies in Hong Kong that have been active in investing in China.
"China will get a high price and they (the assets) will still be controlled by China rather than Hong Kong blue chip companies," he said.
Huan also said red chips are very important to Hong Kong's future economic growth.
Hong Kong returns to Beijing sovereignty on July 1. China is eager to ensure that the transfer of power goes smoothly.
